case: Mahanoy Area School District v. B. L., a minor, by and through her father, Levy, et al.
court_below: United States Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit, 964 F.3d 170
note_on_sources: Primary source is the Supreme Court slip opinion (No. 20-255), read in full. All quotations are transcribed verbatim from that PDF. Secondary sources (Cornell LII, Oyez, Wikipedia) used only to confirm the subject's public name and general framing. The profanity in B.L.'s post is NOT reproduced anywhere in the script; the ledger paraphrases it neutrally.

facts.claim: The case is Mahanoy Area School District v. B. L., No. 20-255, 594 U.S. ___ (2021).
facts.detail: Full caption: 'MAHANOY AREA SCHOOL DISTRICT v. B. L., A MINOR, BY AND THROUGH HER FATHER, LEVY, ET AL.' Argued April 28, 2021; decided June 23, 2021. On certiorari to the Third Circuit (964 F.3d 170).

facts.claim: The subject 'B.L.' is publicly identified as Brandi Levy; she was a minor at the time of the events.
facts.detail: The opinion caption anonymizes her as 'B. L., a minor, by and through her father, Levy.' Her first name, Brandi Levy, is public through her own ACLU-represented advocacy and press coverage. She was 14 at the time of the post. In the documentary she is treated with maximum care: minor at the time, symbolic representation only, no face or likeness, the profane post reframed neutrally.

facts.claim: B.L. was a junior varsity cheerleader who tried out for and failed to make the varsity cheerleading squad.
facts.detail: Opinion: 'Mahanoy Area High School student B. L. failed to make the school's varsity cheerleading squad.' Her second Snap caption referenced being told she needed 'a year of jv before we make varsity,' confirming her JV status. Widely reported as a rising sophomore (she was a freshman going into her sophomore year); the slip opinion itself does not state her grade in words, so the exact 'rising sophomore' label rests on secondary reporting.

facts.claim: The post was made off campus, on a weekend, from a local convenience store, to her private circle of Snapchat friends.
facts.detail: Opinion: 'That weekend, B. L. and a friend visited the Cocoa Hut, a local convenience store. There, B. L. used her smartphone to post two photos on Snapchat... B. L. posted the images to her Snapchat "story"... (B. L. had about 250 "friends")... for a 24 hour period.' The Court later stressed her posts 'appeared outside of school hours from a location outside the school' and were sent 'to an audience consisting of her private circle of Snapchat friends.'

facts.claim: One image showed B.L. and a friend with raised middle fingers and a profane caption venting frustration about school and cheerleading; a second image was a text-only caption about the varsity decision.
facts.detail: NEUTRAL DESCRIPTION (profanity NOT reproduced): The first image showed the two of them with middle fingers raised and a vulgar caption cursing school, softball, cheer, and 'everything.' The second image was blank but for a caption complaining that she and another student were told they needed a year of JV before making varsity, with an upside-down smiley emoji. The Court characterized the posts as 'criticism of the rules of a community of which B. L. forms a part' and noted 'one contained vulgar language and gestures.' The actual profane wording exists in the record but is deliberately omitted from the ledger and script.

facts.claim: The school suspended B.L. from the junior varsity cheerleading squad for the upcoming year (one year).
facts.detail: Opinion: 'When school officials learned of the posts, they suspended B. L. from the junior varsity cheerleading squad for the upcoming year.'

facts.claim: The District Court sided with B.L.; the Third Circuit affirmed but on the broader ground that schools have no special license to regulate any off-campus student speech.
facts.detail: The District Court granted a TRO and preliminary injunction reinstating her, then granted summary judgment, awarding nominal damages and attorneys' fees and ordering her disciplinary record expunged, finding her Snaps had not caused substantial disruption under Tinker. 'The Third Circuit affirmed the judgment, but the panel majority reasoned that Tinker did not apply because schools had no special license to regulate student speech occurring off campus.'

facts.claim: The Supreme Court decided the case 8-1 in B.L.'s favor.
facts.detail: 'BREYER, J., delivered the opinion of the Court, in which ROBERTS, C. J., and ALITO, SOTOMAYOR, KAGAN, GORSUCH, KAVANAUGH and BARRETT, JJ., joined. ALITO, J., filed a concurring opinion, in which GORSUCH, J., joined. THOMAS, J., filed a dissenting opinion.' Eight justices in the majority; Thomas alone in dissent.

facts.claim: Justice Breyer wrote the majority opinion.
facts.detail: Breyer delivered the opinion of the Court, joined by Roberts, Alito, Sotomayor, Kagan, Gorsuch, Kavanaugh, and Barrett.

facts.claim: Justice Alito filed a concurrence joined by Justice Gorsuch.
facts.detail: 'ALITO, J., filed a concurring opinion, in which GORSUCH, J., joined.' Alito agreed with the result but wrote separately to elaborate on the in loco parentis / delegated-parental-authority framework for deciding when a school may reach off-campus speech.

facts.claim: Justice Thomas was the lone dissenter.
facts.detail: 'THOMAS, J., filed a dissenting opinion' (no other justice joined). Thomas argued that historically, under in loco parentis, schools long had authority to discipline off-campus student speech that had a proximate tendency to harm the school, and that B.L.'s speech was directed at classmates and teammates and reached campus.

facts.claim: The anchor precedent is Tinker v. Des Moines Independent Community School District, 393 U.S. 503 (1969).
facts.detail: Tinker established that students retain First Amendment rights at school but that schools may regulate speech that 'materially disrupts classwork or involves substantial disorder or invasion of the rights of others' (393 U.S., at 513).

facts.claim: Verbatim 'schoolhouse gate' language as quoted by Breyer.
facts.detail: Breyer, majority: 'We have made clear that students do not "shed their constitutional rights to freedom of speech or expression," even "at the school house gate." Tinker, 393 U. S., at 506.' The original Tinker sentence (quoted in Alito's concurrence): 'It can hardly be argued that either students or teachers shed their constitutional rights to freedom of speech or expression at the schoolhouse gate.'

facts.claim: Holding: the school violated B.L.'s First Amendment rights, but the Court declined to set a broad, bright-line rule for off-campus speech.
facts.detail: Syllabus 'Held: While public schools may have a special interest in regulating some off-campus student speech, the special interests offered by the school are not sufficient to overcome B. L.'s interest in free expression in this case.' And: 'The school violated B. L.'s First Amendment rights when it suspended her from the junior varsity cheerleading squad.' The Court expressly refused a categorical rule: 'we do not now set forth a broad, highly general First Amendment rule stating just what counts as "off campus" speech and whether or how ordinary First Amendment standards must give way off campus.' The Court did NOT hold that schools can never regulate off-campus speech.

facts.claim: The Court expressly listed categories of off-campus speech schools MAY still regulate.
facts.detail: Verbatim: 'These include serious or severe bullying or harassment targeting particular individuals; threats aimed at teachers or other students; the failure to follow rules concerning lessons, the writing of papers, the use of computers, or participation in other online school activities; and breaches of school security devices, including material maintained within school computers.' In short: serious/severe bullying or harassment of individuals; threats to teachers or students; cheating/rule-breaking on lessons, papers, computer use, or online school activities; and breaches of school security.

facts.claim: Breyer gave three features of off-campus speech that diminish a school's regulatory interest (they diminish, not eliminate, that interest).
facts.detail: Verbatim framing: 'We can, however, mention three features of off-campus speech that often, even if not always, distinguish schools' efforts to regulate that speech.' FEATURE 1: 'First, a school, in relation to off-campus speech, will rarely stand in loco parentis... off-campus speech will normally fall within the zone of parental, rather than school-related, responsibility.' FEATURE 2: 'Second, from the student speaker's perspective, regulations of off-campus speech, when coupled with regulations of on-campus speech, include all the speech a student utters during the full 24-hour day. That means courts must be more skeptical of a school's efforts to regulate off-campus speech, for doing so may mean the student cannot engage in that kind of speech at all.' FEATURE 3: 'Third, the school itself has an interest in protecting a student's unpopular expression, especially when the expression takes place off campus. America's public schools are the nurseries of democracy.' Conclusion: 'these three features... mean that the leeway the First Amendment grants to schools in light of their special characteristics is diminished.'

facts.claim: Verbatim 'nurseries of democracy' passage.
facts.detail: Breyer, majority: 'Third, the school itself has an interest in protecting a student's unpopular expression, especially when the expression takes place off campus. America's public schools are the nurseries of democracy. Our representative democracy only works if we protect the "marketplace of ideas."... That protection must include the protection of unpopular ideas, for popular ideas have less need for protection.'

facts.claim: Why B.L. won on the facts: her speech was off-campus, on her own time, private, targeted no individual, and caused no substantial disruption.
facts.detail: The Court found her posts 'appeared outside of school hours from a location outside the school,' that she 'did not identify the school in her posts or target any member of the school community with vulgar or abusive language,' and that she transmitted them 'through a personal cellphone, to an audience consisting of her private circle of Snapchat friends.' On disruption: the record showed 'at most, 5 to 10 minutes of an Algebra class "for just a couple of days"' and that 'some members of the cheerleading team were "upset"'; that 'alone does not satisfy Tinker's demanding standards.'

facts.claim: The decision did NOT overrule Tinker or hold that off-campus speech is beyond all school authority; it rejected the Third Circuit's categorical rule.
facts.detail: The majority disagreed with the Third Circuit's holding that Tinker never applies off campus: 'we do not believe the special characteristics that give schools additional license to regulate student speech always disappear when a school regulates speech that takes place off campus. The school's regulatory interests remain significant in some off-campus circumstances.' The Court simply declined to define the full scope, leaving line-drawing for future cases. GUARDRAIL against overclaim: do NOT say the Court ruled 'schools can never punish off-campus speech.'

facts.claim: B.L. was represented by the ACLU; the case is the first time the Supreme Court squarely addressed a public school's power over a student's off-campus social-media speech.
facts.detail: The ACLU and ACLU of Pennsylvania represented B.L. Commentators widely describe Mahanoy as the Court's first direct engagement with off-campus, online student speech in the internet era, and the most significant student-speech ruling since Tinker (1969). This is characterization/context (secondary), hence medium confidence on the 'first / most significant' framing; the representation and novelty are well supported but are commentary, not a holding.
